prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of magic-angle flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep B042 as my preferred configuration, but with less confidence than in round 1, and I want to say exactly why I hold it. The Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation is a simple continuum-model argument that made a sharp, checkable statement: near a particular twist angle the low-energy bands of twisted bilayer graphene become nearly flat, so interactions rather than kinetic energy decide the physics. The 2018 experiments by Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulating states and superconductivity at that angle. That sequence of a quantitative prediction followed by a decisive experiment is exactly what I consider a prize-worthy discovery, and it sits squarely within the band-structure reasoning I know well. The result is not the product of one laboratory in isolation, since many groups have reproduced the correlated states and the platform has spread to other graphene multilayers and to transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems. That breadth is my main answer to the maturity objection. The three credited names map onto one prediction and one experimental discovery without forcing anyone out of the three-person limit, and the citation can be written around the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated states, leaving the pairing mechanism aside.
statement.case_against: The round-1 exchange has strengthened the case against my own choice, and I should state it plainly. Five colleagues prefer B046 and give reasons I find scientifically sound: a single sharply defined invention, a two-name credit with clear owners, and clock-to-clock agreement across independent laboratories at the 1e-18 level. B042 is the younger result. The origin of the superconductivity is unsettled and several correlated phases are sample dependent. The credit is also not clean: the experimental discovery involved co-first authors (Cao, Fatemi and others) who are outside the credited names, and earlier continuum-model work on twisted bilayers (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) bears on priority; I cannot resolve either point from the supplied record, and I am recalling this history from memory. Having raised these myself in round 1, I cannot now say that colleagues who weigh them more heavily are mistaken. What I have not heard is an argument that the discovery itself is doubtful. The disagreement is over timing and credit, and on those I stay with an earlier prize on a result I judge deep, but I accept that the case for waiting a few years is a respectable position, not an error.

responses.point: Lindroth says the origin of the superconductivity in magic-angle graphene is still debated, that experimental credit is narrower than the work, and that the lattice clock is more settled because its performance can be compared directly between laboratories.
responses.response: Direct clock-to-clock comparison is the strongest form of verification and I concede B046 has it in a way B042 cannot match. Where I would still separate the two is on what the verification is of. The clock result is a measurement of how well something can be done, while the twisted-graphene result is a statement about what nature does, namely that a nearly flat band produces insulators and superconductors in a system made of carbon alone. I also agree that the credit question is real and I do not claim it is closed. I would defend the three names as the prediction and the discovery, with wording that does not claim the whole moire literature, but I accept that this is a matter of judgment and a narrower experimental credit than the work deserves is a cost.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the magic-wavelength idea with many-atom Lamb-Dicke confinement was not honoured by the 2005 comb prize or the 2012 single-system prize, and that the credit has clear owners, so two names suffice.
responses.response: This answers the overlap worry better than I expected, and it moves me. If the magic-wavelength trapping condition and parallel interrogation of many atoms are what produced the orders-of-magnitude gain in stability, then B046 is a distinct achievement and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 work. My remaining reservation is narrower: much of the later gain is a continuing programme of systematic-uncertainty work, and I would want the citation to rest on the invention and first realisation, which the proposed wording does. I now rank B046 as my first alternative and would not oppose it. My difference with Kroll is about breadth of consequence for physics, not about validity.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B038 as a concept-level organising principle, a Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant band insulators confirmed across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi2Se3, while accepting that the credit chain is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree with the description of the science and I ranked B038 third in opening. His distinction from the 2016 prize, that Z2 invariants protected by time-reversal symmetry without an external field are a different classification from the quantum Hall type phases, is a fair one and weakens the overlap objection I raised. What remains is attribution. A citation that names Molenkamp's HgTe observation while leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose proposal the experiment tested, has a visible gap, and Mehlig himself says so. I note that B042 faces a similar kind of credit problem with Cao and Fatemi, so I do not claim my choice is cleaner on attribution; I claim only that its three-name structure follows one prediction and one experimental discovery, while B038 requires more names than the limit allows to tell the whole story.

responses.point: Olsson moved the lattice clock to the head of her configuration, now lists B042 only as an alternative, and asks whether the committee should wait for twisted bilayer graphene to mature given the pairing question and the credit to Cao and the early continuum-model authors.
responses.response: I understand why the maturity point moved her and I do not think she is wrong to weigh it. We agree on the science: the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated states are secure and the citation should not claim the pairing mechanism. We differ on whether that suffices now. My view is that the discovery is established even though the mechanism is open, and the Prize has often honoured a discovery before its full explanation. Her point about how decisive the experimental credit is, and her concern that the clock priority record cannot be fully verified from the files, both cut across the candidates. If the committee decides to wait, I would want it to be a decision about credit and timing and not a judgment that the discovery is uncertain.

responses.point: Danielsson says the pairing mechanism is disputed and the phase diagram is sample dependent, and that as a theorist he is wary of recognising a field before the superconductivity is understood.
responses.response: As a theorist working on electronic structure I share the wariness, and it is why my citation names the flat bands and the observed correlated states and not a mechanism. I would add that the prediction part of the prize does not depend on the pairing question: the continuum model concerns the band structure and its quenched bandwidth, and that part is borne out. I accept that the sample dependence of the phase diagram is a real limit on how cleanly the experimental half can be stated, and that is the most persuasive part of his case. Where I disagree is in treating an unresolved mechanism as a reason to defer a result whose existence is not in doubt.

responses.point: Pearce treats the lattice clock as an unambiguous instrument-level achievement verified by independent laboratories, and says he ranks B042 low because of timing and attribution, namely the age of the experiments and the credit to Cao and Fatemi.
responses.response: I accept the argument that independent verification is the strongest form of evidence, and B046 meets it. On timing I would only note that eight years from the experiments is a normal interval for a result with a large community behind it, and the reproduction across material families is real. On attribution he is right that the experimental credit is narrower than the work, and the three-name limit forces that. I would not claim to have resolved it. I also want to say that I do not think the number of members preferring B046 should settle the question. I take the argument that it is the cleanest case, and I do not take the count as the argument.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should recognise magic-angle graphene now, with a citation limited to flat bands and observed correlated states, or wait until the superconducting mechanism and the sample dependence of the phase diagram are better understood.

Whether three names can fairly represent the discovery given the experimental co-first authors (Cao, Fatemi and others) and the earlier continuum-model authors; I rely on recollection of this priority history, not on verified sources.

How much of the lattice-clock gain after the first realisation is a separable invention and how much is a continuing systematics programme, which bears on whether two names and the proposed wording are fair.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves enough room for B038, which affects how I rank it as a second alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My work on electronic-structure theory and two-dimensional materials at Uppsala is in a neighbouring area to B042, but no documented personal or institutional connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer is stated, and I have none to disclose for B046 or B038. I chaired the 2025 prize committee, which is relevant to how I weigh B006 against the 2025 prize and not a conflict for the candidates I am discussing. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
